These are quantitiesa are Random Variable Definition 3.1 (Random Variable) Given a random experiment with an outcome space \(S\), a function \(X\) that assigns one and only one real number \(X(s) = x\) to each element \(s\) in \(S\) is called a random variable. The space of \(X\) is the set of real numbers \(\{x: X(s) = x, s \in S\}\), where \(s \in S\) means that the element \(s\) belongs to the set \(S\). A random variable, usually written \(X\), is a variable whose possible values are numerical outcomes of a random phenomenon. A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome in a sample space. Looking it in mathematical function Domain: TT, HT, TH, HH Function, \(X\): The rule you define (i.e. The number of Head) Space of \(X\), Range: 0, 1, 2 Example 3.1 A rat is selected at random from a cage and its sex is determined. The set of possible outcomes is female and male. The outcome space is \(S = \{\text{female}, \text{male}\} = \{F, M\}\). Let \(X\) be a function defined on \(S\) such that \(X(F)= 0\) and \(X(M)=1\). \(X\) is then a real-valued function that has the outcome space \(S\) as its domain and the set of real numbers \(\{x: x= 0, 1\}\) as its range. We call \(X\) a random variable and the space associated with \(X\) is \(\{x: x=0, 1\}\). It may be possible that the set \(S\) has elements that are themselves real numbers. -In such an instance, we could write \(X(s) = s\) so that \(X\) is the identity function, and the space of \(X\) is also \(S\). Example 3.2 The experiment is tossing a die. Probability distribution for a discrete random variable: can be represented by a formula, a table, or a graph, which provides \(P(X) = P(X=x)\) for all \(x\). It assigns nonzero probabilities to only a countable number of distinct \(x\) values. Any value \(x\) not explicitly assigned a positive probability is understood to be such that \(P(X=x) = 0\). The function \(f(x) = p(x) = P(X=x)\) for each \(x\) within the range of \(X\) is called the probability distribution of \(X\). It is often called the probability mass function (p.m.f) for the discrete random variable \(X\). For the p.m.f, \(f(x)\) is positive for at most a countable number of values of \(x\) and satisfies the following properties: \(f(x_i) \ge 0, x \in S\) \(\sum_{x \in S} f(x_i) = 1\) \(P(x \in A) = \sum_{x \in A} P(x), A \subset S\) Example 3.4 We can plot the p.m.f in graphical format \(x\) \(0\) \(1\) \(2\) \(P(x)\) 1/4 1/2 1/4 Exercise 3.2 Let a chip be taken at random from a bowl that contains six white chips, three red chips, and one blue chip. Graph the pmf as a line graph. 3.4 Continuous Random Variable \(X\) is a continuous RV if there exists a nonnegative function \(f(x)\) defined for all real \(x \in (-\infty, \infty)\), having the property that for any set \(B\) of real numbers, \(P(X \in B) = \int_B f(x)dx\). Probability distribution for a continuous random variable: \(f(x)\) is approximately equal to the relative frequency of the interval \(\{x: a < x < b\}\) and hence can be thought of as an estimate of the probability that the RV \(X\) falls into the interval \((a, b)\). This probability is often written as \(P(a < x < b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx\). It is often called the probability density function (pdf) for the continuous random variable \(X\). 3.4.1 Properties of continuous Random Variable Pdf of \(f(x)\) satisfying the conditions: \(f(x) > 0, x \in S\) \(P(X \in (-\infty, \infty)) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)dx = \int_S f(x)dx = 1\) If \(a, b \subseteq S\), then the probability of the event \(\{a < x < b\}\) is \(P(a < x < b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)dx\). Remarks: if \(a=b\), then \(P(x=a) = \int_{a}^{a} f(x)dx = 0\). Example 3.5 Suppose that \(X\) is a continuous random variable whose probability density function is given by: \[\begin{align} f(x) = \begin{cases} C(4x - 2x^2) & 0 < x < 2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{align}\] What is the value of \(C\)? Find \(P(X>1)\). Solution: Since \(f\) is a probability density function, we must have \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)dx = 1\] \[\begin{align} C \int_{0}^{2} (4x - 2x^2)dx =& 1 \\ C \left[2x^2 - \frac{2x^3}{3} \right]_0^2 =& 1 \\ C =& \frac{3}{8} \end{align}\] Hence, \(P(X>1) = \frac{3}{8} \int_{1}^{2} (4x - 2x^2)dx = \frac{1}{2}\). So basically, it is average or mean of the outcomes. Definition 3.3 (Expected Values and Expected Function) The expected value or mean of a random variable \(X\), denoted by \(E(X)\) is: \[\mu = E(X) = \begin{cases} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x)dx & \text{if } X \text{ is continuous} \\ \sum x f(x) = \sum g(x)P(X=x) & \text{if } X \text{ is discrete} \end{cases}\] Example 3.8 (Example 8) Let \(X\) equal number of spots on the side facing upwards after a six-sided die (one of pair of dice) is cast at random. If everything is fair about this experiment, a reasonable probability model is given by the p.m.f. \(f(x) = P(X=x) = 1/6\), where \(x=1,2,3,4,5,6\). Therefore, the expected value of this distribution is: \[\mu = E(X) = \sum_{x=1}^{6} x\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) = 1\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) + 2\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) + 3\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) + 4\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) + 5\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) + 6\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) = \frac{7}{2}\] From previous Example 8, Let \(Y=X^2\), then \(Y\) is also a random variable such that p.m.f of \(Y\) is \(g(y) = P(Y=y) = 1/6\), where \(y=1,4,9,16,25,36\). If \(X\) is a RV, the \(r\)th moment of \(x\) is defined as \(\mu_r' = E[X^r]\). Therefore, the \(r\)th moment about the origin of a random variable is the expected value of \(X^r\): \[\mu_r' = E(X^r) = \begin{cases} \sum_x x^r f(x) \\ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^r f(x)dx \end{cases}\] The first moment is \(E(X)\). Definition 3.5 (Centrol Moments) The \(r\)th moment about the mean of a random variable \(X\), is the expected value of \((X - \mu_X)^r\), symbolically, \[\mu_r = E[(X - \mu_X)^r] = \begin{cases} \sum_x (x - \mu_X)^r f(x) \\ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x - \mu_X)^r f(x)dx \end{cases}\] The \(r\)th moment about the mean of a random variable \(X\) is sometimes called the \(r\)th central moment of \(X\). Note that: * \(\mu_1 = E[(X - \mu_X)] = 0\) * \(\mu_2 = E[(X - \mu_X)^2] = Var[X]\) Variance can be also written as \(\sigma_X^2 = \mu_2' - \mu_X^2\). The first moment is mean of \(E(X)\). The second central moment is the variance. If \(E(X^n)\) exists for some +ve integers \(n\), we call \(E(X^n)\) the \(n\)th moment of \(X\) about the origin. If \(E|X^n| < \infty\) for some +ve real number \(\alpha\), we call \(E|X^n|\) the \(\alpha\)th absolute moment of \(X\). Definition 3.6 (Moment Generating Function (MGF)) Moment generating function \(M(t)\) of the RV \(X\) is defined for all real values of \(t\) by: \[M(t) = E[e^{tx}] = \begin{cases} \sum e^{tx} p(x) & \text{if } X \text{ is discrete} \\ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{tx} \cdot f(x)dx & \text{if } X \text{ is continuous} \end{cases}\] Example 3.11 (Example 11 (Discrete case)) Let the p.m.f. of \(X\) be defined by \(f(x) = x/6\), where \(x=1,2,3\).
